purpose: Prevents untrusted input from being interpreted as code or query logic, covering SQL injection, command injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and related flaws.
summary: Injection occurs when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query, allowing an attacker to trick the interpreter into executing unintended commands or accessing data without authorization; this includes SQL, NoSQL, OS command injection, and cross-site scripting.
expectedStatementElements: How user input is validated, sanitized, and encoded before being used in queries, commands, or rendered output
Whether parameterized queries or an equivalent safe API is used consistently instead of string-concatenated queries
How output is encoded/escaped based on context (HTML, JavaScript, URL) to prevent XSS
How the application is tested for injection vulnerabilities across all input surfaces, including headers and file uploads
evidenceExamples: Code showing parameterized queries or ORM usage instead of raw string concatenation
Input validation and output encoding library/framework configuration
Content Security Policy (CSP) or other XSS mitigation configuration
Security test results (SAST/DAST or manual) covering injection across input surfaces
commonGaps: Some queries are still built through string concatenation rather than parameterization
User input is rendered into HTML or JavaScript without context-appropriate encoding
Input validation exists on obvious form fields but not on headers, file names, or less obvious input surfaces
No systematic testing (automated or manual) specifically targets injection vulnerabilities
interviewQuestions: Are all your database queries parameterized, or are any still built by concatenating strings?
If I entered a script tag into a form field, would it execute when rendered back to another user?
Does input validation cover less obvious input surfaces like headers, cookies, and file names?
Has this application been systematically tested for injection vulnerabilities?
